brief.situation: You maintain the internal policy assistant at Lakeshore Utilities (fictional). To stop wrong answers, last month someone added the whole 60-page operations manual to every prompt. Answers are better, but the bill tripled and answers are slow. The budget review is at 16:00. It is 15:05.
handover: Staff ask about 30,000 questions a month.
The manual is already split into sections and indexed in a knowledge base nobody wired in.
howItWorks: Pick a step from the action list: look, change, check or ship. Nothing you pick is typed or executed: every step shows an authored result.
Each step takes working minutes, and the clock moves by the minutes it takes. The deadline runs on the same clock.
Shipping is final for this case. Afterwards you record what you found and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For finance: why the cost rose, what you changed, and how you know.

parts.label: Why
parts.criteria: On-demand inference bills input and output tokens; each request sent about 46,000 input tokens of manual, 99% of the tokens, which also made answers slow.
parts.modelAnswer: Input tokens dominate cost and latency.

parts.criteria: Retrieve the few relevant sections from the knowledge base and send only those; a smaller model still sends the whole manual and answers worse; capping output barely changes the bill.

parts.label: How you know
parts.criteria: A replay of 1,000 questions projects 1,180 a month with the same answer set score and 3-second answers.

scoring.modelReasoning: Read the usage before changing anything: each request sends about 46,000 input tokens and gets about 300 back, so input drives both cost and latency. Retrieve the few manual sections relevant to each question and send only those, then replay real questions to check cost, quality and latency. A smaller model still pays for the whole manual and answers worse; capping maxTokens trims the 1% that was output.
